description: We’re Sarawak Orbiters, three Sarawakian engineers with backgrounds in aerospace, mechanical engineering, and cybersecurity. We came together with a shared goal of building something that could benefit our communities. When fires and haze blanketed Borneo for months in 2026, robbing over 3,500 lives in September alone, the crisis hit close to home. It inspired us to build IGNIS to aid local responders and authorities monitor, prepare and respond better for the coming fire seasons in the region.
summary:
When haze from the 2026 fires reached hazardous levels in Sarawak, we saw firsthand how fires in one part of Borneo can affect communities across the island. We built IGNIS (Integrated Geospatial Network for Ignition Surveillance) to help fire responders, land managers, and local authorities decide where and when to focus monitoring, patrols, and pre-season preparations.

IGNIS brings more than two decades of NASA satellite records onto a common scale. MODIS and VIIRS detect hotspots at different resolutions, so their raw counts are difficult to compare. Our harmonised metric, H Count, expresses older MODIS observations on a VIIRS-equivalent scale. In West Kalimantan, month-specific adjustments reduced the median error in held-out annual totals from 10.0% to 7.1% compared with a single year-round adjustment.

For any available Borneo district, the Burning Calendar shows when hotspot activity typically rises, the heatmap shows where detections cluster, and Insights shows how unusual a selected month is for that area. Users can explore and share these findings through an interface available in English, Bahasa Melayu, Bahasa Indonesia, and Iban.

We plan to pilot IGNIS in Sarawak, test its transferability in Kalimantan, then adapt it with local partners for northern Peninsular Malaysia and other parts of Southeast Asia.
details:
What happened in Borneo, and why does it matter?

By 9 August 2026, fires had burned about 28,680 hectares in West Kalimantan. Across Kalimantan, NASA satellite data showed 3.4 times as many hotspot detections from 1 January to 15 October 2026 as during the same period in 2023, and 1.7 times as many as in 2019. In September alone, the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimated that exposure to fire smoke contributed to 3,560 deaths across Indonesia. Across the border in Sarawak, the Air Pollutant Index reached a hazardous 519 in Serian on 4 September. For us as Sarawakians, the haze brought home how fires in one part of Borneo can affect communities across the island.

For the people preparing for the next fire season, the question is where does burning repeatedly concentrate, when does it usually intensify, and how early should we prepare? Satellites have recorded hotspots for more than two decades, but the record spans sensors with different detection capabilities. In West Kalimantan, VIIRS S-NPP recorded more than four times as many hotspots as MODIS over their overlap period. A historical chart that switches directly between those counts can make a change in sensor look like a change in burning activity.

What did we build, and who is it for?

IGNIS (Integrated Geospatial Network for Ignition Surveillance) is a web app that helps Borneo’s fire responders, local authorities, and land managers use past fire activity to plan where and when to focus patrols, verify hotspots in the field, and position crews and equipment. It brings more than two decades of NASA hotspot records into one map, one burning calendar, and one harmonised metric called H Count.

Open any available Borneo district and month in IGNIS. The Burning Calendar shows when burning activity usually rises. Compared with the usual shows how that month compares with the historical median for the same calendar month. The map shows where hotspots concentrated, and the export gives a team something it can take into a planning briefing. The views follow the same selected area and dates. IGNIS also removes the language barrier to various communities through its multi-language feature. Users can view the page, its analytics and retrieve comprehensive reports in their own native languages to better understand and prepare accordingly.

Why IGNIS, and why the Sarawak Orbiters?

NASA FIRMS provides the recent detections, fire map, and historical archive that IGNIS builds on. IGNIS brings those records into a district-level planning workflow. A team can move from “Where were hotspots detected?” to “Is that unusual here, and which areas should we prioritise for field checks?” without switching between MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) records or assembling the comparison and briefing separately. FireAId focuses on wildfire risk and resource allocation, while FuelVision maps wildfire fuels. IGNIS focuses on interpreting a district’s observed hotspot history against its own seasonal baseline.

We are three Sarawakian engineers who have experienced transboundary haze firsthand. We built IGNIS around the island’s shared fire history and the boundaries people actually work within. A user can view Kalimantan, Sarawak, Sabah, and Brunei together, then narrow the view to a district or draw their own area of responsibility. The demo interface is currently available in English, Bahasa Melayu, Bahasa Indonesia, and Iban, so users can explore the same map, calendar, and insights in the language they prefer. Starting in Sarawak gives us a place to advocate for the tool directly and learn from the people who would use it in pre-season planning.

What can users do in IGNIS?

How did we harmonise the satellite data?

We used NASA FIRMS records from MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer, aboard Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite, aboard Suomi NPP and NOAA-20). The MODIS product has a nominal resolution of about 1 km, while the VIIRS product is 375 m. Across their overlap in West Kalimantan, VIIRS S-NPP recorded 4.21 times as many hotspot detections as MODIS overall. The ratio varied by month, from 3.65 in July to 5.68 in December, so we tested whether month-specific adjustments would improve comparisons.

H Count expresses the monthly record in VIIRS-equivalent hotspot detections. For each area and month, IGNIS applies the following rule in order:

  1. Use VIIRS S-NPP as observed when it has coverage.
  2. Use VIIRS NOAA-20 divided by 1.01 when only NOAA-20 is available. The adjustment comes from the observed ratio between the two VIIRS records.
  3. Scale MODIS with the factor for that calendar month when only MODIS is available. We fitted each factor by dividing the pooled S-NPP detections by the pooled MODIS detections for that month across the overlap period. Pooling totals limits the influence of individual months with very few detections.

For historical comparisons, IGNIS divides the selected month’s H Count by the median H Count for the same calendar month in other years. A value of 2× means the selected month had double the usual hotspot activity for that area and month. H Count measures satellite detections. In the Hotspot Shifts view, arrows represent movement between observed detection locations, and FRP measures radiative power. The layers support historical interpretation and field verification planning.

For extended harmonisation methodology and analysis, visit our harmonisation file team's GitHub repository at this link here.

How well did the harmonisation work?

We compared four methods in West Kalimantan using the 14 complete overlap years from 2012 to 2025. We held out one year at a time, fitted each method on the other 13 years, and estimated the held-out year’s VIIRS total using MODIS. The fitted factors for the initial West Kalimantan analysis used overlap data through November 2026, while the validation excluded 2026 because it was incomplete.

We selected month-specific factors because they gave the lowest median annual error and kept the adjustment easy to explain. Performance varied by year. The method underestimated the 2020 total by 41%, a year with relatively low fire activity. The 7.1% figure describes held-out annual totals in West Kalimantan. District-level and Borneo-wide performance remain to be evaluated.

How do we scale from Borneo to Southeast Asia?

  1. Pilot in Sarawak. Start where our team has the strongest local ties for outreach and advocacy. Ask district fire responders or land managers to use IGNIS to prepare a pre-season briefing. Measure how long it takes and whether users can independently identify recurring hotspot concentrations, explain an unusual month, and use the evidence to propose priorities for field checks.
  2. Verify the approach in Kalimantan. Take the same workflow to local specialists and prospective users in the region that informed our initial harmonisation study. Check whether results hold at district level and across different fire seasons. Use the findings to decide where regional adjustment factors or different ways of presenting uncertainty are needed.
  3. Expand to northern Peninsular Malaysia, then to other Southeast Asian regions. Reuse the satellite pipeline, calendar, map, and exports. Work with local specialists and developers to validate the sensor adjustments, establish regional fire-season baselines, and review terminology with local speakers. Add features according to local needs, such as terrain and access layers for areas that are difficult to verify in the field, Thai and other local-language interfaces where relevant, and trusted local news and event feeds that help users understand what was happening during an unusual month.

For each new region, we would track how many districts have a locally reviewed setup and whether users can complete the planning task independently. That gives us a way to measure both reach and practical use.

What data, tools, and references did we use?

Data and attribution

  • NASA Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). Used MODIS Collection 6.1 from Terra and Aqua (request 843314), VIIRS 375 m from S-NPP (843315), and VIIRS 375 m from NOAA-20 (843316). Fields used include acquisition time, detection confidence, and Fire Radiative Power. FIRMS archive · FIRMS fire map
  • geoBoundaries. Administrative boundaries for Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei, including district-level datasets where used. geoBoundaries is maintained by William & Mary’s geoLab and licensed under CC BY 4.0. geoBoundaries · Runfola et al. (2020)
  • Esri ArcGIS Online. World Dark Gray Canvas, World Light Gray Canvas, and World Imagery basemaps. Imagery credits include Esri, Maxar, and Earthstar Geographics. Esri basemaps

Tools and implementation

  • Python for aggregating FIRMS detections by month and sensor, fitting the scaling factors, and running the leave-one-year-out comparison. The repository includes burning_calendar.py, harmonization_analysis.py, and ADR 0001, which documents the decision to use VIIRS-equivalent scaling.
  • Leaflet 1.9.4 for the interactive map and geographic overlays. Leaflet
  • ExcelJS 4.4.0 for downloadable Excel workbooks. ExcelJS
  • GDELT DOC 2.0 API and gdeltdoc for local-news exploration. A region-specific news feed is part of the expansion plan. GDELT DOC API · gdeltdoc

AI and production tools used for IGNIS

  • ChatGPT assisted with background research, data analysis, and drafting and refining the project documentation.
  • Claude assisted with code generation, feature ideation, and development of the demo video.
  • Antigravity assisted with code generation for the IGNIS web application.
  • Remotion was used to assemble, animate, and render the demo video.
